Abstract:
<jats:p>Biomaterials encompasses a diverse array of engineering techniques employed for generating materials suitable for repairing or replacing biological structures within living systems. The creation of highly designed materials that can effectively interface with biological systems for tissue and organ replacement, repair, or augmentation is the outcome of latest developments in biomaterials. The primary and paramount prerequisite is the biomaterial's ability to be seamlessly accepted by the human body. The use of biomaterials in medical implants is complemented by biocompatibility as a prominent aspect. Metal alloys, polymers, ceramics, and composite materials are the prevailing material classes frequently utilized in biomedical applications. These four types of materials, either individually or in combination, comprise most implantation devices available in the market today. In numerous domains of biology, surgery, and medicine, the assessment of mechanical properties plays a vital role in determining the significance of biomaterials. This study aims to comprehensively examine key aspects of biomaterial characterization, material selection procedures, mechanical properties, fabrication techniques, and tribological behavior, highlighting their significance in the field of biomaterials. This review offers a thorough summary of the most recent developments in biomaterials, emphasizing their innovative qualities, wide range of industrial and clinical uses, and growing scientific attain. By critically examining the advancements that characterize the state of biomaterial research today, it seeks to provide light on the difficulties, possibilities, and potential paths future.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The scandium modified aluminium alloy Scalmalloy® is specifically developed for the use in laser‐based powder bed fusion (PBF‐LB). It is supposed to show potential in the production of lightweight structures due to its high specific strength compared to other aluminium alloys. A limiting factor is the high surface roughness of additively manufactured parts, which has a negative influence on its mechanical properties, especially under cyclic loads. In order to reduce the surface roughness, methods of design of experiments (DoE) are applied to develop contour parameters. Additionally, the formation of pores in keyhole‐mode welding and strategies to reduce the porosity in the contour area are investigated. The surface roughness of vertical walls can be reduced down to Ra < 7 μm using contour scans with a line energy EL >0.9 J mm−1 but keyhole pores start to form applying EL >0.6– 0.75 J mm−1. Two contour parameter sets in different EL‐ranges are developed that can be used to reduce the surface roughness compared to parameter sets without contour scans, without increasing the porosity in the contour area. Their impact on the mechanical properties has to be further investigated.

Abstract:
<jats:p>The influence of the main process parameters, laser power, point distance and time exposure, on the surface microgeometry of Ti6Al4V specimens produced by a pulsed powder bed fusion process was investigated. A 3D characterization was carried out and collected data were elaborated to reconstruct the surface and to determine both the 3D and the 2D material ratio curves along different directions. The 3D material ratio curve gives a slightly lower material ratio of peak zone Mr1 and higher material ratio of valley zone Mr2, reduced peak height Rpk and reduced valley height Rvk than the 2D curves. Roughness is greater in the 3D analysis than in the 2D one, skewness is the same and kurtosis increases from <3 in 2D to >3 in 3D. Roughness and skewness increase on increasing point distance and decreasing time exposure and laser power. Within the investigated ranges (27.3–71.2 J/mm3), an increase in energy density reduces the surface roughness while skewness and kurtosis are not significantly affected. The results indicate that a 3D approach allows better characterization of the surface microgeometry than a 2D one.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Abstract The quality of metal objects fabricated via laser powder bed fusion are highly affected by process parameters, and their influence on final products is yet to be fully explored. In this work, pyrometry signals of the melt pool were collected from a set of stainless-steel samples during manufacturing and the effect of laser power on porosity and roughness of final printed parts was analyzed. Results show that the melt pool pyrometry signal of contours increases with higher laser power, whereas it is lower and decreases for the infilled part. Post-built X-ray computed tomography imaging reveals that porosity decreases while sample roughness increases upon increasing laser power. The decrease in porosity with increasing laser power is attributed to the larger size of the contour welds that were printed first, leading to an increase in dimension of the final products.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Additive manufacturing (AM) has significantly expanded the design and application of NiTi (Nitinol) alloys in medical devices by enabling the fabrication of complex geometries, fine features, and patient-specific structures that are difficult or impossible to achieve through conventional methods. This review provides a focused and comparative overview of AM technologies applied to NiTi in biomedical devices. This review presents the AM technologies relevant to NiTi, including powder bed fusion (PBF), directed energy deposition (DED), Sheet Lamination (SHL), Material Extrusion (MEX), outlining their operational principles, typical application domains, and suitability for biomedical use. Among these, selective laser melting (SLM), also known as laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB), is identified as the most widely adopted approach for NiTi medical device manufacturing due to its high geometric resolution and ability to produce near-net-shape components. In addition, emerging and non-traditional AM techniques such as binder jetting (BJT), material jetting (MJT), and vat photopolymerization (VPP) are discussed in the context of hybrid and multi-material medical device systems, where they are primarily used to complement NiTi-based functional components rather than directly fabricate load-bearing NiTi structures. The effects of each AM process on the microstructural behavior of NiTi are examined. Future perspectives are discussed, focusing on optimized material design, advanced process control, improved manufacturing equipment, and data-driven approaches to accelerate the translation of additively manufactured NiTi into reliable, high-performance biomedical devices. Overall, this review provides a comprehensive comparison of AM technologies for NiTi in biomedical applications, serving as a reference framework to guide future research and support informed process selection for the development of next-generation biomedical devices.</jats:p>

Abstract:
A novel technique is developed to improve the resolution of two‐photon direct laser writing lithography. Thanks to the high collimation enabled by extraordinary εNZ (near‐zero) metamaterial features, ultrathin dielectric hyper‐resolute nanostructures are within reach. With respect to the standard direct laser writing approach, a size reduction of 89% and 50%, in height and width respectively, is achieved with the height of the structures adjustable between 5 and 50 nm. The retrieved 2D fabrication parameters are exploited for realizing extremely thin all‐dielectric metalenses tailored through deep machine learning codes. The hyper‐resolution achieved in the writing process enables the fabrication of a highly detailed dielectric 3D bas‐relief (with full height of 500 nm) of Da Vinci's “Lady with an Ermine”. The proof‐of‐concept results show intriguing cues for the current and trendsetting research scenario in anti‐counterfeiting applications and ultracompact photonics, paving the way for the realization of all‐dielectric and apochromatic ultrathin imaging systems.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Two-photon polymerization (2PP) is revolutionizing micro- and nanoscale manufacturing by enabling true 3D fabrication with feature sizes far below the diffraction limit—capabilities that traditional lithography cannot match. By using ultrafast femtosecond laser pulses and nonlinear absorption, 2PP initiates polymerization only at the laser’s focal point, offering unmatched spatial precision. This paper highlights key advancements driving the field forward: the development of new materials engineered for 2PP with improved sensitivity, mechanical strength, and the introduction of high-speed, parallelized fabrication strategies that significantly enhance throughput. These innovations are shifting 2PP from a prototyping tool to a viable method for scalable production. Applications now range from custom biomedical scaffolds to complex photonic and metamaterial structures, demonstrating their growing real-world impact. We also address persistent challenges—including slow writing speeds and limited material options—and explore future directions to overcome these barriers. With continued progress in materials and hardware, 2PP is well positioned to become a cornerstone of next-generation additive manufacturing.</jats:p>

The confinement of a material to a two-dimensional plane is a significant bottleneck in achieving ultra-high recording densities, and this has led to the proposition of three-dimensional (3D) racetrack memories that utilize domain wall propagation along the nanowires. Abstract Micro/nano-fabrication technology via two-photon polymerization (TPP) nanolithography is a powerful and useful manufacturing tool that is capable of generating two dimensional (2D) to three dimensional (3D) arbitrary micro/nano-structures of various materials with a high spatial resolution. This technology has received tremendous interest in cell and tissue engineering and medical microdevices because of its remarkable fabrication capability for sophisticated structures from macro- to nano-scale, which are difficult to be achieved by traditional methods with limited microarchitecture controllability. To fabricate precisely designed 3D micro/nano-structures for biomedical applications via TPP nanolithography, the use of photoinitiators (PIs) and photoresists needs to be considered comprehensively and systematically. In this review, widely used commercially available PIs are first discussed, followed by elucidating synthesis strategies of water-soluble initiators for biomedical applications. In addition to the conventional photoresists, the distinctive properties of customized stimulus-responsive photoresists are discussed. Finally, current limitations and challenges in the material and fabrication aspects and an outlook for future prospects of TPP for biomedical applications based on different biocompatible photosensitive composites are discussed comprehensively. In all, this review provides a basic understanding of TPP technology and important roles of PIs and photoresists for fabricating high-precision stimulus-responsive micro/nano-structures for a wide range of biomedical applications.

This study proposes a straightforward and precise method for fabricating micro/nano structures with morphological gradients utilizing single-voxel synchronous control and a nano-piezoelectric translation stage in a two-photon laser direct writing technique. To address the defocusing issue in large-scale fabrication, a methodology for laser focus dynamic proactive compensation was developed based on fluorescence image analysis, which can achieve high-precision compensation of laser focus within the entire range of the nano-piezoelectric translation stage. Additionally, the fabrication of hexagonal lattice periodic structures assembled from morphological gradient needle structures and the size gradient Archimedean spiral structures validate the capability of the single voxel-based fabrication and proactive focus compensation method for complex gradient structure fabrication.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The propensity to manufacture functional and geometrically sophisticated parts from a wide range of metals provides the metal additive manufacturing (AM) processes superior advantages over traditional methods. The field of metal AM is currently dominated by beam-based technologies such as selective laser sintering (SLM) or electron beam melting (EBM) which have some limitations such as high production cost, residual stress and anisotropic mechanical properties induced by melting of metal powders followed by rapid solidification. So, there exist a significant gap between industrial production requirements and the qualities offered by well-established beam-based AM technologies. Therefore, beamless metal AM techniques (known as non-beam metal AM) have gained increasing attention in recent years as they have been found to be able to fill the gap and bring new possibilities. There exist a number of beamless processes with distinctively various characteristics that are either under development or already available on the market. Since this is a very promising field and there is currently no high-quality review on this topic yet, this paper aims to review the key beamless processes and their latest developments.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Metal additive manufacturing (AM) has emerged as a critical manufacturing route for producing geometrically complex metallic components; however, its structural application is limited by strong process–structure–property coupling and defect-driven reliability concerns. This review provides a rigorous and integrated analysis of metal AM technologies by quantitatively and mechanistically linking fabrication conditions with microstructural evolution, mechanical response, and long-term performance. Primary processing routes including powder bed fusion, directed energy deposition, and binder jetting are evaluated in terms of energy density, melt pool dynamics, and thermal gradients that govern solidification kinetics. The response of key alloy systems (steels, aluminum alloys, titanium alloys, and nickel-based superalloys) is examined with respect to phase transformation pathways, grain morphology (columnar vs. equiaxed), texture development, and defect formation mechanisms such as porosity, lack of fusion, and keyholing. The influence of these microstructural features on anisotropic mechanical behavior, including tensile strength, fatigue life, and fracture resistance, is critically analyzed. Emphasis is placed on the role of thermal history and cyclic reheating in generating residual stresses and microstructural heterogeneity, which directly impact reliability under service conditions. The effectiveness of post-processing techniques such as heat treatment and hot isostatic pressing in modifying defect populations and enhancing structural integrity is also assessed. Current limitations in process repeatability, standardization, and predictive modeling are identified, highlighting the need for integrated in-situ monitoring, physics-informed modeling, and data-driven optimization. This review establishes a mechanistic framework for understanding and improving the reliability of metal additive manufacturing in structural applications.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Efficient waste management practices are becoming increasingly necessary due to the negative environmental and health impacts of waste generation and disposal. One type of waste that has received particular attention is electronic waste (e-waste). This category of waste has the potential to cause significant environmental harm if not disposed of properly. The management of e-waste is crucial in the electrical/electronic industry which has led to the creation of models and institutional legislature to promote sustainable production processes. Among these processes, Additive manufacturing otherwise referred to as 3D printing is particularly effective in reducing waste generation and energy requirements by reusing spent parts and products as feedstock. Sustainability in the manufacturing and production sectors can be promoted through the inculcation of certain practices. Of these practices, reusing e-waste that would otherwise be disposed of in landfills has the potential to promote environmental cost savings. This article introduces the potential of e-waste being integrated into the manufacturing sector to promote sustainable production. The article also addresses the problem of geometric e-waste generation and suggests an efficient way of reusing waste from the electrical and electronic industries.

Abstract:
The present paper reports on the development of a biodegradable overmolded orthopedic implant: a metal bone fixing screw, which has been overmolded with a functionalized thin layer of biodegradable polymer to enhance cell adhesion during the healing process. The main challenges were to integrate precise, high-throughput and repeatable solutions to achieve a thin, defect-free structured polymer layer and to ensure a high and consistent implant quality. The work carried out entailed determining proper materials (Purasorb PDLG 5010) for the biodegradable overmolding layer and its economical substitute (NaKu PLA 100HF) to be used during initial tool and process development, designing the surface structure of the overmolded polymer layer, development of injection molding tools, as well as feeding and handling procedures. The injection overmolding process of Purasorb PDLG 5010 polymer was controlled, and the process parameters were optimized. In particular, the dominant process parameters for the overmolding, namely injection pressure, barrel temperature and mold temperature, were experimentally examined using a circumscribed three-factor central composite design and two quality marks; overmolding roughness and mass of polymer. The analysis of the experimental results shows that the mass of the overmolding is not feasible for use as the quality mark. However, the optimal parameters for the overmolding of a metallic implant screw with a thin, micro-structured polymer layer with a predefined roughness of the surface texture have been identified successfully.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Développement et caractérisation de mélanges polymères-poudres métalliques pour le micro moulage par injection</jats:title>
                <jats:p xml:lang="fr">Le micro-moulage par Injection de Poudres (Micro-PIM) est l’une des technologies permettant de réaliser des micro-composants de très petites dimensions, associés à la miniaturisation et la fonctionnalisation dans différents domaines d’applications. La thèse concerne l’élaboration et la caractérisation de mélanges basés sur des poudres d’acier inoxydable de type 316L, l’identification des paramètres physiques associés à l’étape de densification est traitée. Des modélisations physiques et des simulations numériques de l’étape de densification par diffusion à l’état solide, sont ensuite proposées.De nouvelles formulations de mélanges à base de liants polymériques ont été développées pour différentes granulométries de poudres d’acier inoxydable de type 316L (5 µm et 16 µm). Les différents mélanges élaborés ont été élaborés et validés grâce à des comparatifs entre couples de mélangeages et courbes de viscosité de cisaillement. Les mélanges élaborés avec une formulation de base composée de polypropylène, de cire paraffine et d’acide stéarique, sont adaptés pour les deux types de poudre, et conduisent à des résultats significatifs pour les différents tests réalisés, conduisant à un couple de mélangeage et à une viscosité de cisaillement relativement faibles par rapport aux autres formulations. Le taux de charge critique obtenu pour l’acier inoxydable 316L (5 µm), avec la formulation optimale, est de 68% et a été déterminé par différentes méthodes. Les essais de micro-injection pour le mono-matériau (316L mélange) et les bi-matériaux (mélange de 316 L et Cu) ont été analysés en détail. Des tests d’homogénéité ont été réalisés avant et après l’étape d’injection.Un modèle thermo-élasto-viscoplastique approprié pour modéliser l’étape de densification a été utilisé pour la simulation de la densification des micro-composants. Les paramètres d’identification du modèle physique ont été identifiés pour des mélanges de poudres d’acier 316L (5 µm), pour différents taux de charge (62%, 64% et 66%). Des essais de flexion 3 points et de compression ont été réalisé à l’intérieur d’un dilatomètre vertical avec trois cinétiques de densification (5 °C/min, 10 °C/min et 15 °C/min). Les résultats obtenus par dilatométrie, ont permis l’identification du module de viscosité de cisaillement G, du module de compressibilité K, et de la contrainte de densification σs, Le modèle de comportement associé à la densification, incluant les paramètres identifiés a été implémenté dans le code éléments finis Abaqus©. Des éléments finis adaptés ont été utilisés, tant pour le support, que les quatre micro-éprouvettes de référence. Les simulations de l’étape de densification pour trois différentes cinétiques (5 °C/min, 10 °C/min et 15 °C/min) à 1200°C, ont été réalisées pour l’ensemble des micro-composants dont les taux de charge correspondent respectivement à 62%, 64% et 66%. Les retraits et densités relatives des micro-composants obtenus par simulation sont en très bonne corrélation avec les résultats expérimentaux</jats:p>

Abstract:

 For many decades, experimental solid mechanics has played a crucial role in characterizing and understanding the mechanical properties of natural and novel materials. Recent advances in machine learning (ML) provide new opportunities for the field, including experimental design, data analysis, uncertainty quantification, and inverse problems. As the number of papers published in recent years in this emerging field is exploding, it is timely to conduct a comprehensive and up-to-date review of recent ML applications in experimental solid mechanics. Here, we first provide an overview of common ML algorithms and terminologies that are pertinent to this review, with emphasis placed on physics-informed and physics-based ML methods. Then, we provide thorough coverage of recent ML applications in traditional and emerging areas of experimental mechanics, including fracture mechanics, biomechanics, nano- and micro-mechanics, architected materials, and 2D material. Finally, we highlight some current challenges of applying ML to multi-modality and multi-fidelity experimental datasets and propose several future research directions. This review aims to provide valuable insights into the use of ML methods as well as a variety of examples for researchers in solid mechanics to integrate into their experiments.

Abstract:
Heat-performance nickel-based superalloys are commonly applied in various critical industries. In this work, test samples in the form of turbine blades were manufactured by means of laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) 3D technology. This research focused on comparison of the influences of various surface finishing methods. The mechanical surface post-processing of the LPBF-manufactured Inconel 718 alloy samples consisted of ultrasonic impact treatment (UIT), ultrasonic shot peening (USP), shot peening (SP), and barrel finishing (BF). The surface microrelief was evaluated using a high-precision laser profilometer, while the microstructural features were studied by light optical microscopy (LOM), scanning/transmission electron microscopy (SEM/TEM), and X-ray diffraction (XRD). Potentiodynamic polarization tests were also conducted to compare the surface finishing methods in terms of corrosion resistance improvement of the LPBF-manufactured 718 alloy samples. The effects of the surface microstructure and hardening intensity in combination with residual stresses and surface relief coupled with roughness profile shapes on the room temperature corrosion behavior of plastically deformed 718 alloy specimens manufactured by LPBF were studied. The corrosion rate (CR) of the LPBF-manufactured samples was reduced after post-processing: BF (~16 μm/year), USP (~15 μm/year), SP (~6.5 μm/year), and UIT (~5.5 μm/year). The experimental trends also agreed well with the theoretical trends of uniform corrosion of the studied alloy.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Significant advances have been made in the field of Additive Manufacturing (AM) across various manufacturing processes. Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) is one of the most widely adopted metal AM processes in the industry, which employs energy sources such as lasers to melt powder materials. While the LPBF process offers numerous advantages, such as the ability to produce complex geometries and multiple parts simultaneously, it also presents challenges in the form of defects such as porosity, residual stresses, and cracks that need to be addressed. Conducting experiments to identify and eliminate these defects can be prohibitively expensive, motivating the development of alternative predictive approaches. Numerical modeling and simulation techniques provide a cost-effective alternative to experimental approaches, enabling analyses ranging from thermal histories and microstructural evolution to mechanical property prediction and defect identification in fabricated components. However, such simulations can also be computationally intensive. In recent years, Machine Learning (ML) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) algorithms have emerged as viable alternative tools to accelerate process understanding, defect prediction, and parameter optimization. This review provides a comprehensive overview of ML-based approaches applied to LPBF, emphasizing the importance of understanding the underlying physical phenomena that significantly influence data collection, preprocessing, and feature engineering strategies essential for effective model training and validation. It offers a structured framework for researchers seeking to leverage ML methods to enhance predictive accuracy and computational efficiency, particularly through simulation-driven data generation for model development.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The prediction of porosity is a crucial task for metal based additive manufacturing techniques such as laser powder bed fusion. Short wave infrared thermography as an in-situ monitoring tool enables the measurement of the surface radiosity during the laser exposure. Based on the thermogram data, the thermal history of the component can be reconstructed which is closely related to the resulting mechanical properties and to the formation of porosity in the part. In this study, we present a novel framework for the local prediction of porosity based on extracted features from thermogram data. The framework consists of a data pre-processing workflow and a supervised deep learning classifier architecture. The data pre-processing workflow generates samples from thermogram feature data by including feature information from multiple subsequent layers. Thereby, the prediction of the occurrence of complex process phenomena such as keyhole pores is enabled. A custom convolutional neural network model is used for classification. The model is trained and tested on a dataset from thermographic in-situ monitoring of the manufacturing of an AISI 316L stainless steel test component. The impact of the pre-processing parameters and the local void distribution on the classification performance is studied in detail. The presented model achieves an accuracy of 0.96 and an f1-Score of 0.86 for predicting keyhole porosity in small sub-volumes with a dimension of (700 × 700 × 50) µm3. Furthermore, we show that pre-processing parameters such as the porosity threshold for sample labeling and the number of included subsequent layers are influential for the model performance. Moreover, the model prediction is shown to be sensitive to local porosity changes although it is trained on binary labeled data that disregards the actual sample porosity.

## 1. segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 1-2 (Context ID: pqac-00000018)

                                                                                                      3Dresyns Engineering Publications · ER-149

Lithography-Based Metal Manufacturing: Metal-Filled Photoresins,
Cure–Loading Trade-Offs, Debinding, Sintering and Qualification
Optical–Rheological Coupling, Green-State Evidence and Complete-Cell Control

3Dresyns by Resyner Technologies S.L.
Juan Segurola
Correspondence: [email redacted] · Website: www.3Dresyns.com
Engineering Review · ER-149 · Version 0.2 · 5 September 2026

Statement of Significance
   Lithography-based metal manufacturing can shape fine metal-rich features by patterned photopolymerisation without melting metal in
the printer. The apparent precision of projected light does not remove the material difficulty: metal powder must remain dispersed in a
binder that can be coated or renewed, transmit or redistribute enough light to create a controlled green layer, release from the exposure
interface, survive recovery and cleaning, open safe transport paths during binder removal and densify without unacceptable chemistry
change or distortion. Powder loading, viscosity, yield stress, thixotropy, sedimentation, absorption, scattering, cure depth, lateral overcure
and green strength are not independent controls. Nor is a support-free green print necessarily support-free in the furnace. This review
defines the route as a complete indirect chain from released powder, binder and optical system to an accepted metal component. It
separates green photopolymer conversion from debinding and metallurgical densification, bounds published high-resolution and material
demonstrations to their tested systems, and replaces printer-centred claims with part-linked factory evidence.

Abstract
   Lithography-based metal manufacturing uses patterned light to solidify a photoactive metal-powder/binder system layer by layer,
producing a green composite that is subsequently cleaned, debound and sintered or otherwise densified. Literature labels such as LMM,
LMAM, metal DLP, micro-DLP and metal stereolithography cover related but not necessarily identical material-delivery and exposure
architectures. Liquid suspensions, thixotropic pastes and temperature-conditioned feedstocks impose different mixing, sedimentation,
recoating, separation and recovery burdens. Increasing metal loading can reduce organic content and support final densification, while
increasing viscosity, reducing layer renewal and changing optical attenuation and scattering. A nominal wavelength, pixel pitch or scalar
dose cannot predict cured geometry without the spectrum, irradiance map, powder/resin optical state, initiator response, exposure
sequence and measurement method. The exposed object remains a green metal–polymer composite; cure depth, green strength and
apparent feature fidelity do not establish final metal. Binder removal  is governed by chemistry, transport length, gas evolution,
atmosphere and evolving pore pathways. Sintering changes dimensions, pores, chemistry and microstructure under gravity and setter
interaction, so shrinkage cannot be qualified by one scale factor. This qualitative engineering review maps material preparation, light
delivery, green recovery, debinding, densification, factory economics, safety, inspection and qualification. It provides no transferable
formulation, exposure, cleaning, furnace, compensation or acceptance recipe.
Keywords: lithography-based metal manufacturing; metal DLP; vat photopolymerisation; metal-filled photoresin; cure depth; green part;
debinding; sintering; shrinkage; qualification

1. Purpose and scope
  ISO/ASTM 52900 defines vat photopolymerisation as an additive-manufacturing category in which liquid photopolymer in a vat is
selectively cured by light-activated polymerisation [1]. ER-149 addresses the indirect metal subset in which patterned exposure retains
metal powder inside a photoreactive organic phase. The printer creates a green composite, not molten, bonded or service-ready metal. The
delivered metal state exists only after declared recovery and cleaning, binder removal, sintering or another densification operation,
cooling, finishing and inspection.
   The scope includes metal-powder and binder receipt, photoinitiator/absorber/dispersant and additive control, mixing, deagglomeration,
degassing, storage, sampling, temperature conditioning, suspension or paste renewal, layer coating or recoating, optical exposure,
separation or platform movement, green release, unexposed-feedstock removal, cleaning, support or raft removal, green storage and
inspection,  solvent/water/catalytic/thermal  binder  removal  where  specified,  brown-state  control,  sintering,  setters,  dimensional
compensation, optional HIP or heat treatment, machining, surface treatment, cleaning, inspection, production economics, safety and
qualification.
   The terms `lithography-based metal manufacturing`, `lithography metal additive manufacturing`, `metal DLP`, `micro-DLP` and
`stereolithography of metals` are used only with the implementation described by the cited source. They do not establish an identical vat,
film, paste-delivery, recoating, exposure or separation mechanism. NIST treats VPP as an architecture requiring light and material
metrology rather than a generic exposure-time setting [13]. The 2026 NIST photopolymer workshop report likewise identifies unresolved
measurement, data, safety and standards gaps across photopolymer AM [14].
   Polymer VPP is assigned to ER-142. In that route the post-cured network is the delivered material. ER-149 instead removes the
photoactive organic phase and thermally consolidates powder. Metal binder jetting and bound-metal extrusion belong to ER-147 and
ER-148; they form green geometry by binder placement in a powder bed or by deposition of a pre-compounded road. Ceramic VPP
belongs to ER-151. Polymer-binder powder-bed shaping belongs to ER-155. Laser/electron-beam PBF and DED/WAAM belong to
ER-145, ER-146 and ER-150 because they melt metal during deposition or layer consolidation.
   The industrial selection gate and the direct-versus-indirect route distinction are inherited from ER-139 and ER-049 [11,36]. ER-044
owns photoabsorbing fillers, optical response and cure-depth control; ER-036 owns rheology, recoating and dispersion in highly filled
VPP suspensions; ER-034 owns separation and peel mechanics; ER-031 owns cure shrinkage, residual stress and warpage; and ER-037

                                                 3Dresyns Engineering Publications · ER-149 · 2026 · Page 1                                                                                                      3Dresyns Engineering Publications · ER-149


owns debinding-defect formation in photopolymer-derived ceramic and metal green bodies [39–43]. ER-149 does not restate those
owners. Its own question is whether a metal-filled, photoactive, layer-delivered system at the loading required for later sintering can
maintain a qualified optical–rheological window through green recovery and then enter a metal-specific debinding/sintering chain without
losing geometry, chemistry, pore-state or factory control. Open-vat oxygen inhibition and stabilisation chemistry are inherited from
ER-030 and ER-032 [37,38]; ER-149 extends them only where metal powder, reservoir history, green conversion and later binder removal
interact. These boundaries preserve the LMM-specific industrial question while preventing duplicate ownership.
   Castable photopolymers for investment casting are not equivalent to powder-loaded LMM. The printed object in a castable route is a
sacrificial pattern, while the final metal is produced by a mould-and-casting chain. The 3Dresyns LMM instructions explicitly distinguish
reactive binder routes intended for debinding/sintering from castable routes intended for jewellery-related indirect manufacture [35]. This
paper uses that page only to define declared workflow scope, never as independent proof of compatibility, performance or safety.
   This review does not prescribe powder chemistry or size, surface treatment, solids loading, binder composition, dispersant, initiator,
absorber, mixing sequence, viscosity, yield stress, temperature, wavelength, irradiance, exposure, layer thickness, recoating speed,
separation motion, cleaning medium, debinding route, furnace atmosphere, thermal ramp, peak temperature, hold, shrink factor, setter
material, HIP cycle or acceptance limit. Each value belongs to a specified powder–binder–light-engine–delivery–geometry–thermal-route
–intended-use state.

2. Process identity and the state-resolved production chain
   The word `printing` hides several material identities. A released metal powder and released organic ingredients become a filled
photoactive system. That system may be fluid at rest, shear-thinning, thixotropic, temperature-conditioned or paste-like.  It is then
distributed as a controlled layer or exposure interface. Patterned

separation motion, cleaning medium, debinding route, furnace atmosphere, thermal ramp, peak temperature, hold, shrink factor, setter
material, HIP cycle or acceptance limit. Each value belongs to a specified powder–binder–light-engine–delivery–geometry–thermal-route

photoactive system. That system may be fluid at rest, shear-thinning, thixotropic, temperature-conditioned or paste-like.  It is then
distributed as a controlled layer or exposure interface. Patterned radiation converts only part of the binder network, retaining a local
particle architecture. The recovered green object still contains binder, unreacted species and powder whose distribution was established
during formulation, layer delivery and cure.

   The chain prevents three common category errors. First, polymerisation is a geometry-retention reaction, not metal fusion. Second,
unexposed material can support a green feature during shaping without becoming a qualified removable support strategy. Third, thermal
debinding and sintering can occur in one furnace programme while remaining different transformations with different failure modes.





                                     Figure 1. State-resolved lithography-based metal-manufacturing route.

    Traceability crosses batch and load boundaries. One feedstock batch can supply multiple builds; one build can contain multiple
exposure-field positions; one debinding or sintering load can combine parts from several builds; external thermal processing can add
organisational custody changes. The genealogy links powder and binder lots, mixing and ageing history, vat/reservoir and coating state,
light-engine map, file/version and build position, green handling, cleaning, furnace load/position, setter, post-processing, tests and final
serial/batch. ISO/ASTM 52951 and 52953 provide data-package and monitoring-registration architecture, but they do not decide which
signals constitute acceptance [8,9].
   For purchased components, ISO/ASTM 52901 requires the provider and customer to define feedstock, final characteristics, inspection,
acceptance and documentation  [6]. A purchase order that asks only for “metal DLP 316L” leaves the green and thermal route

underdefined. It should state the delivered condition, required chemistry and properties, surface and cleanliness state, critical geometry,
test coverage and allowed post-processing.

3. Metal powder, photoactive binder and filled-feedstock release
   The metal powder brings alloy chemistry, particle morphology, size distribution, surface oxide or adsorbates, packing behaviour and
contamination history. The organic phase brings reactive monomer or oligomer, photoinitiator, inhibitors, absorbers, dispersants, diluents,
plasticising or rheology-modifying functions. Their combination is not a neutral carrier around powder: it establishes both the green
network and the chemistry/transport burden that must later be removed.
  ISO/ASTM 52907 structures metal-powder characterisation [12]. Those methods can inform powder identity and condition before
mixing, but do not qualify optical attenuation, dispersion, paste stability, layer formation or debinding. A powder released for PBF, binder
jetting, MIM or bound-metal extrusion is not automatically suitable for a photoactive suspension. Surface chemistry that is acceptable
during direct melting may inhibit or accelerate polymerisation, change dispersant adsorption or increase oxygen/moisture sensitivity in an
LMM formulation.
   Solids loading is a system variable rather than a ranking. A higher metal volume fraction may reduce organic mass to remove, increase
green powder packing and reduce the densification distance. It can also increase viscosity or yield stress, reduce recoating speed, trap air,
magnify agglomeration, limit cure penetration and weaken interlayer contact. A lower loading may improve flow or cure while increasing
binder burden, shrinkage and the risk that the green particle network loses continuity during debinding. Scheibler et al. measured coupled
effects of loading, particle size, exposure and orientation on green copper specimens [27]. Their results support a multidimensional
window, not one preferred loading.
   Powder size affects more than nominal resolution. Finer powder can enable thin layers or fine geometries, yet raises surface area,
dispersant demand, viscosity, oxidation/adsorbate sensitivity and potential exposure during handling. C

magnify agglomeration, limit cure penetration and weaken interlayer contact. A lower loading may improve flow or cure while increasing
binder burden, shrinkage and the risk that the green particle network loses continuity during debinding. Scheibler et al. measured coupled
effects of loading, particle size, exposure and orientation on green copper specimens [27]. Their results support a multidimensional
window, not one preferred loading.
   Powder size affects more than nominal resolution. Finer powder can enable thin layers or fine geometries, yet raises surface area,
dispersant demand, viscosity, oxidation/adsorbate sensitivity and potential exposure during handling. Coarser particles can reduce specific
surface and change scattering, while limiting layer thickness or fine feature reproduction. Alazzawi et al. showed in silver and alumina
suspensions that cure depth depended on dispersion/agglomeration, particle size, solids content, refractive index and extinction [20]. The
valid conclusion is coupled optical/material control; the tested values do not transfer to 316L, copper, NiTi or tungsten.
   Dispersion must be tested across scales. A visually uniform reservoir can contain agglomerates, entrained air, settling gradients or
particle/binder segregation. Mixing energy and time can break agglomerates while heating, incorporating gas, changing inhibitor content
or damaging sensitive powder surfaces. Milling media and vessels can add contamination. A controlled batch record defines order of
addition, equipment, atmosphere where relevant, energy/time history, temperature, degassing, filtration or screening, sampling locations
and allowable hold/rework.
   Pan et al. studied dispersant-dependent stability and cure behaviour in a defined 316L slurry [24]. Wu et al. developed a thixotropic
316L paste and linked formulation, stability, cure and final properties in one route [25]. Those studies demonstrate that dispersion,
rheology, light response and thermal conversion can be engineered together. They do not authorise copying the dispersants, loadings,
viscosities, exposure or furnace conditions into another powder, binder or machine.
    Stability is time- and history-dependent. Sedimentation can create powder-rich and binder-rich regions; a thixotropic network can
resist settling at rest but must recover reproducibly after coating shear. Temperature changes viscosity, reaction kinetics and particle
mobility. Repeated circulation, scraping, replenishment or heating can change the mixture. Feedstock release therefore includes a defined
age, container position, conditioning procedure, sampling plan and allowed exposure to light, air and heat.
   Reclaimed unexposed material is not automatically virgin equivalent.  It may carry cured debris, fines, contamination, changed
initiator/inhibitor balance, solvent or cleaning carryover, altered particle distribution and a different light/thermal history. A reuse rule
specifies segregation, screening, refresh ratio where applicable, testing and maximum history. Yield calculations count rejected or
downcycled material rather than labelling all surrounding paste recoverable.

4. Optical attenuation, oxygen inhibition, scattering and the cure–loading trade-off
   ER-044 owns general photoabsorber/filler effects on optical response and cure depth [39]. ER-149 retains only the metal-specific
extension:  conducting,  absorbing  or  reflecting  particles  at  a  solids  loading  intended  to  survive  debinding  and  sintering.
Photopolymerisation requires enough absorbed photons in the intended volume to create a network that retains that powder and connects
layers. The binder, initiator and absorber also shape the spectrum-dependent response. The result is a three-dimensional exposure field
whose boundaries need not align with projector pixels or the commanded layer plane.
   In an unfilled resin, a fitted working curve can relate cured depth to exposure for a declared method. Even there, it is not an immutable
material constant. Kolibaba et al. found large interlaboratory variation when multiple laboratories measured aliquots from one resin batch
[18]. Differences in procedure, hardware, fitting and measurement changed the inferred parameters. A metal-filled system adds particle
scattering, absorption, agglomeration and spatial composition, so transfer becomes still less defensible.
   Nominal wavelength is also insufficient. Caplins et al. showed that spectral bandwidth and the resin absorption gradient can make a
monochromatic interpretation inadequate [19]. A  light engine must be characterised by spectrum, irradiance,  spatial uniformity,
divergence or numerical-aperture context, focus/distortion and stability at the relevant interface. Their earlier light-engine mapping work
demonstrated position-dependent  irradiance/spectral behaviour and  printed response  in one LCD system  [17]. The  transferable
requirement is registration of a measured optical field, not an assertion that one architecture is uniformly superior.
   Metal loading can simultaneously increase the amount of final material per green volume and reduce optical penetration. Cure depth
may fall, while lateral scattering or reflection enlarges a line or closes a gap. Pan et al. quantified pronounced scattering in their studied
316L slurry [24]. Scheibler et al. used single-layer exposure and green bending tests to connect copper loading, particle size and exposure
to cure thickness and green strength [27]. A process window must therefore include both insufficient cure and excessive cure. More
exposure is not a universal correction: it can increase lateral overcure, heat, stress, feature closure or adhesion to an interface while still
failing to cure uniformly through a thick, compositionally non-uniform layer.

   Wieckowski and Erb varied particle, resin and light variables in photoabsorbing filled resins and showed that cure depth can be
changed through multiple coupled routes [21]. Their framework reinforces a qualification sequence: characterise particle and resin optical
response; choose a compatible light package; measure rather than assume a working curve; then verify representative lines, gaps, holes,
walls and layers. It does not define one optimal particle size, wavelength or initiator concentration.
   Cure depth is not the same as network conversion or green strength. A layer can appear continuous at its boundary while containing a
conversion gradient. Sarkar et al. simultaneously measured conversion, stress, temperature and shrinkage during photopolymerisation and
showed that cure protocol changes network state [22]. Metal-filled systems can further redistribute light and heat. Green release therefore
specifies minimum state evidence tied to handling and debinding, rather than a single measured thickness.
   ER-030 and ER-032 own the general radical-photopolymerisation account of oxygen inhibition and open-vat stabilisation [37,38]. In
the LMM-specific extension, dissolved or interfacial oxygen scavenges propagating radicals and forms less-reactive peroxyl species. The
result may be an induction period or a conversion threshold rather than a constant scalar dose penalty. Oxygen transport from the free
surface, a permeable film or a re-aerated reservoir can therefore create a depth or interface gradient; degassing can shorten the induction
state, but transfer, recoating and dwell can restore it. Phenolic or other stabiliser packages interact with this radical balance, so a changed
powder surface, binder lot, headspace, film permeability, degassing history or reuse fraction can move the cure window even when
commanded irradiance and exposure are unchanged. Reservoir atmosphere, degassing/re-aeration interval and interface condition are
registered variables, and their change triggers recalibration of conversion and green release rather than an assumed exposure offset.
   Green conversion is difficult to measure in a highly filled, strongly absorbing body. Transmission infrared may lack a usable optical
path; attenuated-total-reflection sampling is surface-limited and particle-confounded; and calorimetry must resolve a minority organic
phase against dominant metal filler. A production plan therefore declares whether conversion is measured directly or inferred from
qualified surrogates. Permissible candidates include extractables or residual-monomer analysis on a witness geometry; solvent resistance
or swelling under a fixed procedure; green mechanical response under a declared test; or thermal analysis on a deliberately under-loaded
witness formulation whose loading difference is recorded as a validi

set.
   Green conversion is difficult to measure in a highly filled, strongly absorbing body. Transmission infrared may lack a usable optical
path; attenuated-total-reflection sampling is surface-limited and particle-confounded; and calorimetry must resolve a minority organic
phase against dominant metal filler. A production plan therefore declares whether conversion is measured directly or inferred from
qualified surrogates. Permissible candidates include extractables or residual-monomer analysis on a witness geometry; solvent resistance
or swelling under a fixed procedure; green mechanical response under a declared test; or thermal analysis on a deliberately under-loaded
witness formulation whose loading difference is recorded as a validity boundary. Each is labelled a surrogate, not conversion itself, and is
calibrated to the relevant location and geometry with uncertainty, detection limits and correlation to both handling survival and later
debinding behaviour. Cure depth, visual continuity or one green-strength value is never silently relabelled as conversion.
   Optical dose accumulates across layers and neighbouring features. Light intended for a new layer can penetrate into earlier material;
scattered radiation can expose adjacent regions; anti-aliasing or grayscale changes local history. Small islands, thin walls, large solid
cross-sections, edges and closely spaced channels do not share one exposure environment. Calibration artefacts include those geometries
and positions, and their green and final states are measured separately.

5. Rheology, sedimentation, layer delivery and material renewal
   ER-036 owns general rheology, recoating and dispersion control for highly filled VPP suspensions [42]. ER-149 narrows the question
to the solids-loading, powder-surface and time-history state needed to leave a sinterable metal skeleton after binder removal.
   Layer formation asks a filled system to flow, level or transfer under a controlled stress and time, then resist sedimentation or drainage
long enough for exposure. A low apparent viscosity can aid renewal but permit settling or edge flow. A high viscosity or yield stress can
retain particles while trapping air, resisting levelling and increasing blade, film or separation loads. Thixotropy can provide both flow
under shear and recovery at rest only if the recovery time matches the machine sequence.
   Rheology must be reported with method, geometry, shear history, temperature and time. A single viscosity at an unspecified shear rate
cannot predict coating. Yield stress inferred by one fitting model may not equal the stress distribution in a doctor blade, gap, roller,
reservoir or moving platform. Oscillatory recovery, creep or step-shear tests can be useful when connected to actual machine events.
Feedstock qualification links these measurements to layer thickness, surface uniformity, particle distribution and green outcomes.
    Material-delivery architectures differ. A liquid-vat route may require bulk recirculation, recoating and separation through a fluid
suspension. A paste route may use a blade, roller, moving carrier or temperature-conditioned transfer. A feedstock that resolidifies or
rebuilds structure between layers may provide green support while increasing renewal and interface sensitivity. The equipment record
declares the architecture instead of using `LMM` as a complete mechanism description.
   Coating creates gradients. Particle migration, wall slip, filtration at a narrow gap, agglomerate exclusion, meniscus behaviour and
evaporation can alter the layer relative to the reservoir. A blade that produces a visually smooth surface can still create local thickness or
composition differences. Temperature across the reservoir, coating element and exposure interface must be mapped where  it affects
rheology or polymerisation.
   Sedimentation control is not proved by a short observation in a static vial. A production job imposes vibration, periodic shear, stops,
replenishment and exposure heat. The qualification interval covers the longest intended dwell, restart and job duration, with samples from
positions that could become powder-rich or binder-rich. Pan et  al. and Wu et  al. provide material-specific examples of stability
engineering [24,25]; their measured times and values remain bounded to their systems.
   Air and volatile content matter. Bubbles can interrupt a layer, scatter light and become green or sintered pores. Vacuum degassing can
remove air while changing volatile composition or accelerating settling. Mixing and recovery from a partially used batch can reintroduce
gas or debris. The work instruction therefore controls degassing endpoint, post-degassing handling and the interval before use.
   Because degassing also changes the oxygen-inhibited induction state, the material-release record includes reservoir headspace,
interface permeability where relevant and the time/shear history by which the feedstock can re-aerate [37,38]. A change in any of those
conditions invokes optical/green-state recalibration; it is not cleared solely by absence of visible bubbles.
   Renewal time contributes to cycle time. Whole-field exposure may illuminate many parts simultaneously, but a larger or more viscous
cross-section can change separation, coating, levelling, temperature and material transport. A thin exposure does not imply a thin factory
cycle. Throughput claims must include the slowest required layer renewal and downstream operation.

6. Exposure architecture, working curves and feature formation
   ER-034 owns general bottom-up separation and peel mechanics [41]. ER-149 addresses only separation of a powder-loaded layer
whose green strength is a handling and debinding-entry property rather than the service property of a delivered polymer component.
   The exposure system converts digital geometry into an irradiance field at the material interface. Projector micromirror pitch,
magnification and focus can define a sampling grid, but pixel pitch is not final feature resolution. Optical blur, distortion, divergence,
scattering, threshold conversion, overcure, shrinkage, layer registration, green cleaning and sintering all modify geometry. A `35 µm
feature` demonstrated in one study is not a general equipment class.
   Melentiev et  al. demonstrated a high-resolution 316L route with fine features, complex hollow structures and measured final
surface/properties [26]. The study is important evidence that a complete metal-DLP chain can achieve such outcomes in its tested system.
Its resolution, lack of printed supports and final properties remain conditional on its feedstock, machine, geometries, cleaning and thermal
route. They cannot be assigned to another metal or LMM platform by process name.
  A working-curve campaign begins with measured  light delivery and a released feedstock. Single-layer thickness and  lateral
dimensions are measured over relevant dose and position, but the result is only a screening map. Multilayer artefacts then test interlayer
contact, cumulative exposure, small islands, thin walls, gaps, holes, contours and large cross-sections. Green conversion or a declared,
uncertainty-bearing surrogate, together with strength, sets the lower processing boundary; visual continuity alone does not. Excess growth,
trapped material, separation damage and loss of negative features set the upper boundary. The campaign records reservoir atmosphere,
degassing/re-aeration history and exposure-interface permeability where these can alter the inhibition gradient [37,38].
   Exposure-field stitching or tiled projection adds another state where present. Overlap, intensity mismatch, geometric distortion and
timing can create seams. A homogeneous flat field does not prove consistent cure in a filled medium whose temperature or composition
varies across the build. Position-aware coupons and registered monitoring are required.
   Separation mechanics depend on whether the exposed layer contacts a window, film, carrier, bath surface or prior feedstock layer.
Cross-sectional area, viscosity, adhesion, motion and interface condition can affect force and damage. A process with surrounding paste
support can still experience detachment or distortion at the exposure interface. Window/film wear, contamination or clouding changes
optical and mechanical behaviour simultaneously.

systematic error can remain hidden in average dimensions while closing a critical channel or changing a lattice strut. Calibration is
therefore geometry- and position-aware. Software, antialiasing, grayscale,

7. Green recovery, support claims, cleaning and state release
   The green body must be separated from surrounding unexposed material and the machine interface without cracks, delamination,
bending or surface loss. Green strength depends on binder network, conversion, powder loading, geometry, layer contacts and time. It is a
release property for handling and downstream survival, not a metal performance metric.
   Surrounding suspension or paste can support overhangs during exposure in some architectures. The statement `no printed supports` is
therefore plausible for specified features, but incomplete. Unexposed material must drain, be wiped, displaced or dissolved from surfaces
and internal passages. A narrow, blind, tortuous or closed feature that exposes successfully can fail the cleaning gate. The design file must
provide recovery access and a verifiable cleanliness method.
   Cleaning is a material transformation. Solvent or aqueous contact can extract unreacted species, swell or plasticise the green binder,
mobilise particles, leave residue or cause differential stress. Mechanical wiping or jetting can damage fine features. Drying can create
gradients or surface deposits. A qualified cleaning sequence names the medium, purity, agitation/flow, temperature, time, exchange,
drying and reuse/disposal rules, but this review supplies none of those values.
   Printed green supports, rafts and sacrificial features serve build or handling functions. They can also obstruct cleaning or create
damage during removal. Furnace setters serve a later purpose: supporting the weak brown/sintering body while allowing binder gases and
shrinkage. A green support removed before debinding cannot control sintering sag. A setter that prevents sag can constrain contraction,
mark or contaminate a surface.
   Green inspection includes mass or density where validated, dimensions, surface, visible damage, feature clearance, residual unexposed
feedstock and relevant internal evidence. Bulk green density does not resolve a local agglomerate, binder-rich zone or partially cleaned
cavity. Computed tomography or other imaging may be useful when resolution/contrast are adequate, but a non-detection is not proof
below the method capability.
   Storage and transfer can change the green state. Light, heat, oxygen, humidity and residual solvent can continue reaction or alter
mechanical behaviour. A green part may creep under its own weight or a fixture. Time between printing, cleaning and debinding is
therefore controlled, and transport packaging supports the part without blocking volatile release or adding contamination.
  A green release record identifies build, position, feedstock batch/history, optical state, direct conversion method or declared surrogate,
measurement uncertainty, cleaning lot, inspection result, supports/fixtures, deviations and authorisation to enter debinding. Passing it does
not pre-accept the final metal. It prevents known green defects from entering a furnace load where they become harder and more
expensive to diagnose.

8. Debinding and brown-state control
   ER-037 owns the cross-route thermal-debinding mechanisms, hazard taxonomy and general qualification logic [43]. ER-149 inherits
that framework and narrows this section to the distinctive entry state created by LMM: a particle-filled, spatially non-uniform photocured
network whose crosslinking, cleaning residue, powder/binder distribution and optical history determine transport paths into the brown
state. The industrial task here is to establish that this specific green state can enter the ER-037 framework without concealed conversion
gradients or metal-specific chemistry loss; it is not to duplicate the corpus-wide debinding review.
  A binder may contain fractions intended for water or solvent extraction before thermal pyrolysis. Catalytic or direct thermal routes
may be used in other systems. For an LMM green body these choices begin from an exposure-defined network and are not
interchangeable: compatibility depends on crosslink distribution, powder surface, section thickness, feature openness, cleaning history,
support and furnace state. The 3Dresyns IFU declares separate water- and solvent-debindable binder-route families and explicitly assigns
user validation of the actual solids and workflow [35]. It does not prove that either route is complete or suitable for a particular metal.
   The initial green network can affect debinding beyond total organic mass. Overexposure may increase crosslink density or change
accessibility; undercure can leave weak regions; conversion gradients can create non-uniform decomposition. Cleaning residues can alter
local transport. ER-031 owns general cure-shrinkage, residual-stress and warpage mechanics [40]; the LMM-specific extension is that
shrinkage of a constrained binder around comparatively rigid particles can generate interfacial and packing-scale stress before thermal
shrinkage. That stress can open microcracks, weaken particle bridges or create non-uniform transport paths that later amplify gas-pressure
damage during debinding [22,23,40]. Exposure strategy is therefore a debinding-entry variable because it sets part of the interfacial stress
population on which binder removal acts. A debinding model that begins from nominal binder percentage alone is incomplete.
   Small-sample thermogravimetric or evolved-gas analysis can screen the actual LMM feedstock, but the qualification link is geometry-
and load-specific because optical conversion and cleaning accessibility establish the starting transport field. Roumanie et al. linked
debinding/sintering conditions to copper composition and thermal conductivity in one highly loaded photocurable route [28]. Melentiev et
al. investigated faster crack-free debinding and later sintering of thin-walled 316L metamaterials within a defined system [29]. Their
outcomes remain bounded to those formulations, metals and geometries.
   The brown body can be weaker than the green body after polymer support is lost and before metallurgical necks mature. It can crack
during transfer, setter adjustment or early furnace motion. Some factories may integrate thermal debinding and sintering in one
programme, but the brown transition still exists physically. A defined hold point can rely on mass change, gas response, thermal record,
witness specimens, chemistry or other route-specific evidence.
   The LMM brown-state hold links feedstock batch, spatial conversion or declared surrogate, cleaning state, part section/feature family,
furnace load/location, mass or gas evidence, chemistry and integrity. A completed time–temperature trace alone cannot show that the
photocured network was removed uniformly or that metal chemistry remained acceptable. Binder, powder-surface or conversion changes
also trigger renewed exhaust/condensate and contamination assessment under the ER-037 framework [43].

affect densification, grain/phase evolution, chemistry, dimensions and properties. The route is not a low-temperature metal printer

9. Sintering, shrinkage, setters and dimensional compensation
    Sintering forms metallurgical bonds and reduces pore volume through temperature- and time-dependent transport. Powder chemistry
and surface condition, green packing, residual binder, atmosphere, thermal profile, part geometry, load position and setter interaction
affect densification, grain/phase evolution, chemistry, dimensions and properties. The route is not a low-temperature metal printer
followed by generic firing.
   Shrinkage begins from the spatial green architecture. Local powder fraction, agglomerates, cure and cleaning can vary. During
debinding, organic removal creates pore pathways and may rearrange particles. During sintering, neck growth and pore closure interact
with gravity, thermal gradients and friction. The result can be anisotropic and geometry-dependent even when a nominal bulk scale factor
appears stable.
   Compensation models may include axis factors, local feature offsets, anticipated sag, setter contact and final machining stock. They
are trained on representative parts and load/furnace locations, then tested on independent geometry. A model fitted to one alloy, thickness
or orientation is not a universal machine correction. Any powder, binder, exposure, cleaning, furnace, setter or software change can
invalidate it.
    Setters must carry the part as its stiffness falls and it contracts. A broad contact can resist sag while increasing friction and constraining
in-plane shrinkage. A point or rib support can reduce contact while concentrating load or leaving marks. Setter chemistry, surface, reuse
and contamination are controlled. Sacrificial features and separable powder beds can be considered only after their gas-flow, shrinkage
and cleanliness effects are qualified.
    Pressureless sintering, sinter-HIP, separate HIP, heat treatment and infiltration produce different states. HIP can reduce some internal
porosity but cannot restore a missing feature, remove trapped contamination or automatically correct chemistry. Heat treatment can
change strength or corrosion behaviour without eliminating geometric defects. Reports and drawings name the actual delivered state.
   Copper routes  illustrate atmosphere and chemistry sensitivity. Roumanie et  al. linked thermal conditions to composition and
conductivity [28]; Ye et al. followed a pure-copper slurry route through oxidation, densification and conductivity [33]; Lyu et al. reported
a separate high-resolution copper stereolithography route [34]. These studies are not interchangeable recipes. Their collective lesson is
that final conductivity and density depend on formulation, oxygen/carbon control, pore state and the complete thermal history.
   NiTi creates another boundary. Cohen  et  al. demonstrated sinter-based LMM of a NiTi shape-memory alloy and identified
carbon/phase sensitivity in the tested route [31]. A successful 316L or copper binder and furnace path therefore does not establish NiTi
phase transformation, composition or functional response. The same restriction applies to refractory and reactive materials.
   Dimensional acceptance names the state. Green, cleaned, brown, as-sintered, HIPed, heat-treated, machined and finished dimensions
answer different questions. A drawing and report that omit state make compensation and conformance ambiguous. Stable final dimensions
require part and load evidence, not only a shrinkage percentage from coupons.

10. Material windows, pore state, microstructure and properties
    Metal-filled VPP/LMM has been demonstrated for several material systems, but each result belongs to a particular powder, binder,
optical route, geometry, cleaning and thermal chain. Material breadth is evidence of research possibility, not proof that a shared feedstock
architecture can print `any metal`.
    Stainless-steel 316L has the widest evidence in this source set. Pan et al. coupled slurry preparation, scattering, cure and thermal
conversion [24]. Wu et al. coupled a stable paste with cure and final tensile behaviour [25]. Melentiev et al. demonstrated high-resolution
complex structures [26] and separately examined thin-walled metamaterial debinding/sintering [29]. Pires et al. compared supplied micro-
DLP specimens with binder-jet and laser-fused 316L using microstructure, density, surface and mechanical tests [30]. These results
support multiple viable 316L routes, not one universal density, surface, tensile property or feature limit.
   Comparisons require matched states and specimens. Pires et al. reported differences related to density, surface and grain state, while
noting supplier-proprietary process details and different specimen scales [30]. A micro-tensile specimen, standard coupon and final thin-
walled component do not have identical surface-to-volume ratio, defect sensitivity or test uncertainty. Route ranking without matched
geometry, surface, thermal state and method is weak evidence.
   Copper studies demonstrate optical and thermal challenges without defining one best route. Scheibler et  al. focused on green
cure/strength [27]; Roumanie et al. on debinding/sintering, composition and thermal conductivity [28]; Ye et al. on a pure-copper slurry
route [33]; and Lyu et al. on another stereolithographic process/property window [34]. Powder oxide, organic residue, porosity and
atmosphere can dominate conductivity. A green feature result cannot be converted into final electrical or thermal performance.
   Cai et al. demonstrated DLP processing of tungsten through a water-based precursor and multistage thermal route [32]. The work
broadens the evidence boundary to a refractory metal while remaining formulation-specific. It does not establish that conventional metal-
powder photoresins, debinding cycles or inspection methods transfer to tungsten.
   Density is necessary for many applications but not sufficient. Equivalent bulk density can hide different pore size, shape, connectivity
and location. A surface-connected pore can govern leakage or corrosion; an aligned internal defect can govern fatigue; a closed pore may
respond differently to HIP. Archimedes density, image area fraction and CT have different sampling, resolution and uncertainty.
Acceptance selects methods against the failure mode.
   Microstructure  reflects  the thermal  route.  Sintered 316L can show equiaxed  grains and annealing twins  rather than PBF
melt-pool/cellular structures, as observed in the bounded comparison by Pires et al. [30]. That difference is descriptive, not inherently
superior. Grain size, phase balance, inclusions, carbon/oxygen/nitrogen, porosity and heat treatment must meet intended-use requirements.
   Mechanical, thermal, electrical, magnetic, corrosion, fatigue, creep or shape-memory claims require state-specific tests. ISO/ASTM
52927 structures main-characteristic and corresponding test-method selection [7]. It does not convert a literature coupon into a product
guarantee. Evidence must include orientation, surface, geometry, environment, sample count, uncertainty and genealogy.

11. Geometry, surface, inspection and monitoring
  LMM can make fine green features because patterned exposure avoids the melt-pool scale of fusion processes and can expose many
pixels in parallel. That conditional capability does not mean every digital feature survives cleaning, debinding and sintering. Positive
walls, negative gaps, blind holes, open channels, lattices and large solid sections have different exposure, cleaning and thermal risks.
   The minimum printable positive feature and minimum cleanable negative feature are separate quantities. Scattering and lateral
overcure can enlarge a wall while closing a gap. Cleaning can erode a thin wall or leave paste in a channel. Sintering can round, sag or
close a feature. Qualification maps digital, green, cleaned and final geometries rather than quoting projector pixel pitch.
   Surface state inherits layer thickness, optical edge response, coating marks, particle size, cleaning, support/raft removal and sintering.
A low final roughness reported by Melentiev et al. [26] is evidence for their route. It is not a guarantee for another orientation, alloy,
section or finishing state. Surface measurement reports cutoff/filter, direction, area/line method and whether inaccessible surfaces were
included.

12. Complete-cell productivity, economics, safety and environment
   Exposure time is only one interval in the factory cell. The route includes powder and binder preparation or purchase, sampling,
conditioning, reservoir loading, layer renewal, exposure, separation, part recovery, unexposed-material removal, cleaning, drying, green
inspection, debinding queues, debinding, transfer where applicable, sintering, cooldown, setter removal, heat treatment/HIP where
specified, finishing, cleaning, inspection, rework, scrap and release.
   Effective cell throughput, Tcell = Naccepted / tcomplete-cell, reports accepted components per complete elapsed factory-cell time.
 Material efficiency, ηmaterial = maccepted-parts / mreleased-input, is a separate mass ratio. Neither metric substitutes for the other;
              both declare boundary, period, queue state and disposition of recovered, rejected and downcycled material.
   Whole-field exposure can reduce dependence of exposure time on part count within one image, but nesting, cross-sectional area, layer
renewal, separation and thermal capacity still matter. A full plate of thin parts may expose efficiently and overload cleaning or furnace
fixturing. A single thick component may print successfully and become the debinding bottleneck. Cycle models use accepted yield and
queue capacity rather than ideal exposure speed.
   Feedstock preparation can dominate development or changeover. Mixing, deagglomeration, degassing, stability testing, vat cleaning
and contamination clearance require labour and equipment. Purchased proprietary feedstock can move that burden to the supplier while
increasing supply-chain and equivalence risk. A qualified incoming test remains necessary.
   Recovered unexposed material can reduce waste only when its identity and history remain controlled and it can be reused without
degrading output. Cleaning media, contaminated wipes, cured debris, filters, purge/feedstock residues, failed green parts, debinding
condensate, furnace fixtures and finishing waste remain. Environmental claims require a declared boundary, mass balance, energy/utilities
and accepted yield.

14. Conclusions and research priorities
   Lithography-based metal manufacturing is not optical metal fusion. It is patterned formation of a metal-filled photopolymer green
body followed by binder removal and metallurgical densification. Its potential for fine geometry and smooth surfaces comes from a
coupled powder–binder–light–layer system whose optical and rheological demands compete. The green object must then be recovered and
cleaned without damage, converted to a porous brown body without internal pressure or residue, and sintered under controlled gravity,
setter and atmosphere conditions.
  A defensible industrial programme follows five rules:
 1. qualify powder, photoreactive binder, additives, mixture and delivery architecture as one time-dependent feedstock system;
 2. measure spectrum, irradiance field, scattering, cure depth, lateral growth and green state instead of transferring wavelength, dose or
    pixel pitch;
 3. keep exposed, cleaned green, brown, sintered, HIPed, heat-treated, machined and delivered states separate;
 4. qualify cleaning access, debinding, shrinkage, setters and final properties on representative geometry and furnace loads; and
 5. compare LMM with other routes using accepted complete-cell throughput, safety, yield and part-linked evidence.
    Priority research should improve in-line dispersion and sedimentation metrology; rheology-to-layer-transfer models for suspension and
paste architectures; three-dimensional light transport in metal-filled media; spatially resolved conversion metrology for highly loaded and
opaque green bodies; validated conversion surrogates with uncertainty and debinding correlation; oxygen/stabiliser and degassing/re-
aeration maps at permeable interfaces; conversion and particle-packing maps; optical-field calibration tied to final geometry; non-
destructive detection of trapped feedstock and green cracks; geometry-aware cleaning and debinding transport; brown-state monitoring;
shrinkage/setter/friction models; small-feature inspection with quantified probability of detection; material-specific chemistry control for
copper, NiTi, tungsten and other advanced metals; and transfer protocols across feedstock batches, machines and furnaces.

The excerpt describes nanoscale additive manufacturing of metals and related inorganic materials using two-photon lithography and associated laser-based processes. A nickel-cluster-containing hybrid photoresist enables complex three-dimensional nano-architected metals, including nanocrystalline and nanoporous nickel nanolattices, at approximately 100 nm resolution. A cationic photoresist, TP-EO, combined with a bimolecular photosensitizer–photoacid generator system, supports high-throughput 2PP with features below 200 nm, writing speeds up to 100 mm/s, minimal shrinkage, and centimeter-scale nanodevice fabrication. The passage also reports metal-organic photoresists that can be post-sintered into high-purity metal oxides—including ZnO, CuO, and ZrO2—with critical dimensions as small as 35 nm, as well as co-confined 2PP achieving 30 nm critical dimensions and 100 nm lateral resolution. Related materials and processes include nanolamellar high-entropy alloys produced by laser powder bed fusion. The excerpt does not provide a specific overall build volume, nor does it discuss hydrogel infusion of additively manufactured metal parts.
